items.name: STOP technique card
items.body:
A four-step routine for the moment before you react.
Use this whenever you notice anger starting to build.
Stop - pause before you do or say anything.
Take a breath - one slow breath in, one slow breath out.
Observe - what am I feeling, and how strong is it?
Proceed - choose what to do next, rather than reacting automatically.

items.body:

"Can I have a minute before we carry on?"
"I don't agree, but I'm willing to talk about it."
"I need some space, I'll come back to this."

items.name: Nicotine cycle diagram
items.body:
How the nicotine cycle works.
1. Craving builds: the brain signals it wants nicotine
2. Use: vaping delivers a fast hit of nicotine
3. Short dopamine boost: a brief feel-good effect
4. Dip: the feeling fades, often below where it started
5. Craving builds again: the cycle repeats

items.name: Trigger difficulty ranking card
items.body:
Some triggers are harder to resist than others.
• Social triggers (friends offering) are often the hardest to resist
• Emotional triggers (boredom, stress) can sneak up unnoticed
• Habit triggers (same time, same place) are easiest to plan around
• Naming a trigger doesn't mean acting on it, it just makes it visible

• "Maybe later", and just don't come back to it.

items.name: What counts as cyberbullying briefing card
items.body:
Cyberbullying can take many forms.
• Being excluded from group chats deliberately
• Nasty comments or messages, repeated or one-off
• Sharing embarrassing content without consent
• Impersonation or fake accounts
• It can follow you home: that makes it different from in-person bullying

items.name: Block, report, save evidence step card
items.body:
Steps to take if something happens online.
• 1. Take a screenshot before doing anything else.
• 2. Block the person or account.
• 3. Report it on the platform.
• 4. Tell a trusted adult what happened.

items.name: Privacy settings checklist
items.body:

• Is my location shared anywhere?

19.title: Safeguarding: exploitation and county lines awareness

items.name: What makes a relationship feel safe? briefing card
items.body:
Features of a healthy relationship.
• Mutual respect and equal say
• No pressure to keep secrets from people who care about you
• A 'no' is respected without punishment
• You feel like yourself around them, not smaller

items.name: Grooming and exploitation tactics card set
items.body:
Common tactics, explained plainly.
• Being singled out for special attention
• Gifts or money that create a sense of obligation
• Being isolated from friends or family
• Being told to keep secrets from people who care about you

items.name: Why it's hard to spot briefing note
items.body:
These tactics work because they don't feel wrong at first.
• Attention can feel flattering before it feels controlling
• Small favours can build a sense of debt gradually
• Isolation often happens slowly, one friendship at a time
• It's never the young person's fault if this happens to them

items.name: Assertive refusal script cards
items.body:
Clear, simple ways to say no.

• "I'm not comfortable with this."
• "I need to go now."
• No explanation is ever required.

items.body: My calm-down toolkit. Pick one that works for you.

cards.title: Slow breathing: 4 in, 6 out
cards.text: Breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds, then out through your mouth for 6.

cards.title: Ask for a movement break
cards.text: Walk to the water fountain and back, or once around the corridor.

cards.title: Count backwards from 20
cards.text: Count down in your head, slowly, one number per breath.
cards.note: Start again if you lose track

cards.title: Go to my safe space
cards.text: Go to the place you agreed with staff, and stay until it settles.

cards.title: Cold water on my hands
cards.text: Run cold water over your hands and the inside of your wrists.

cards.title: Squeeze a stress ball
cards.text: Squeeze hard for 5 seconds, then let go completely. Your fists work too.

cards.title: Ask for 2 minutes of quiet
cards.text: Ask for 2 minutes with no talking and no questions.
cards.note: Set a timer if it helps

cards.title: Talk to my trusted adult
cards.text: Find the adult you named and tell them how you're feeling.

"I felt left out when I wasn't invited, and I need to know why."
"I felt angry when my things were taken, and I need them back."

items.name: Tally card
items.body: Mark a tally each time you call out or talk over instructions. Add up your total at the end of each lesson.

items.name: Stop-think-choose technique card
items.body:
A simple routine for the moment before you speak.
Use this three-step routine when you notice the urge to call out.
Stop - pause before you speak.
Think - what do I actually want to say or ask?
Choose - use my agreed signal instead of calling out.

items.name: Signal card options
items.body: Choose one with your class teacher.

items.name: Self-monitoring chart
items.body: Rate your self-control each lesson, 1 (hard) to 5 (great).

items.name: Teacher briefing note
items.body:
To hand to the pupil's class teacher.
• This pupil is working on reducing calling out and talking over instructions, as part of a 5-week mentoring
course.
• We've agreed a signal (see 'Signal card options') for the pupil to request your attention instead of calling
out - please respond to it consistently where possible.
• The pupil is using a self-monitoring chart to rate self-control each lesson - a brief, positive comment from
you at the end of the lesson helps reinforce this.
• Please let the mentor know of any patterns you notice, good or otherwise.

items.name: Trusted-adult discussion prompts
items.body:
Questions to explore trust and respect.
Use these to open a conversation, not as a checklist.
Who is an adult you trust, in or out of school?
What makes that relationship feel different?
What's one thing an adult could do that would make you more likely to listen to them?

items.name: Respectful disagreement script card
items.body:
Tone, timing and wording for disagreeing respectfully.
Structure: state what you disagree with, calmly, at the right moment - not in front of the whole class.
"Can I talk to you about this after the lesson?"
"I don't think that's fair, can you explain why?"
"I hear you, but can we find another way?"

items.name: Restorative conversation prompt card
items.body:
Questions to repair a staff relationship.
Use these questions calmly, one at a time.
What happened?
What were you thinking at the time?
Who has been affected, and how?
What would help this relationship going forward?

items.name: Low-pressure activity ideas
items.body:
For the mentor to choose from in Week 1 - let the pupil pick.
• A drawing or colouring activity with no pressure to talk.
• A simple shared game (cards, a puzzle, a quiz).
• A conversation about the pupil's own interests - games, shows, music, sport.
• A shared task, such as tidying or organising something together, which allows conversation without eye
contact.
